## Overview

The reference object is a **live collaborator cursor in Google Docs or
Figma**: when someone else is editing alongside you, you don't see their name
hovering over every keystroke — you see a small colored marker, assigned to
them for the session, and nothing else. You learn "blue is Sam" once, by
memory, not by re-reading a label each time blue does something. That trade
only works because the room is small; add thirty collaborators and blue stops
meaning anything in particular, because some other Sam-adjacent hue is now in
the mix too.

`PureChatList.vue` makes the identical bet for chat. It is the most radical
theme in this project because it is the only one that removes the nickname
entirely — not shrinks it, not de-emphasizes it, deletes it. What is left of
"who said this" is `identity-dot`: a `{spacing.dot-size}` (`1.2rem`) circle,
`{rounded.dot}` rounded into a true circle, filled with `{colors.primary}` —
one sample from the hashed-hue family described under Colors. There is no
plate behind the message either. The message text is the only other thing on
screen, carried entirely by `TextWithShadow`'s hard outline rather than by any
backing surface. This theme is for overlays where the message is what the
audience should be looking at, and the roster of regular chatters is small
enough that a viewer can actually learn "cyan is that one regular" — the same
condition that makes the collaborator-cursor pattern work, and the same
condition whose absence breaks it.

This theme is one of ChaosRat's design systems living under
`app/components/themes/` — self-contained, not a skin over a shared system —
and the invariants every theme must honor regardless of its own look are
recorded in the repo-root `DESIGN.md`'s Overlay Contract & Theme Map section.

## Colors

`{colors.primary}` is written as a single value (`hsl(200, 100%, 70%)`) but
that is a **sample, not a palette entry**. `PureChatList.vue` computes it live,
per author, as `hashToColor(hashCode(chat.nickname), 100, 70)`, which resolves
to `hsl(<hash(nickname) % 360>, 100%, 70%)` — fixed saturation and lightness,
a hue that walks the full 360° wheel keyed off the author's name.
`hashCode`'s `% 360` step means this is a **360-way family**, not a curated
set: two different nicknames can and sometimes will land on the same hue, and
when that happens the dot stops distinguishing them. That is a real,
un-fixable limit of this design, not a bug — accept it as the cost of a
one-color identity system, and don't "solve" it by widening the dot into
something that could hold a second differentiator; the whole point is that it
stays this small.

`{colors.text}` — opaque white — is the message color, and it is the _only_
color in this theme with a fixed value; there is no background pairing for it
to sit against. `.chat-container` renders no plate, no card, no fill of any
kind behind `.message` — the canvas is the transparent overlay itself. That is
why `components.message` in this file declares `textColor` alone with no
`backgroundColor`: pairing it with one would assert a relationship this theme
does not have. Legibility instead comes entirely from `TextWithShadow`'s
8-direction outline (rendered at `shadow-size="0.1"`, i.e. `0.1rem` per
direction, default black shadow color) baked around every glyph — a
mechanism, not a color, so no static WCAG ratio can be computed for
`{colors.text}` here: there is no fixed backdrop to measure it against, only
whatever the OBS scene happens to be compositing at that instant. The same is
true of `identity-dot`'s `{colors.primary}` fill: it sits directly on live
video with nothing behind it either, held legible by its own `0.2rem` solid
`rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.1)` ring (see Shapes) rather than by contrast against a
background. There is no `border`/`borderColor` property in this schema to
bind that ring to, so it is recorded here in prose instead of as a token.

## Typography

`{typography.message}` is the only typographic role this theme needs, because
there is no nickname text to style separately. Its `fontFamily` is the
project's shared Pretendard-led sans stack; this file restates it in full
because token references resolve only within the same file — there is no
cross-file inheritance from the root `DESIGN.md`, even though the underlying
CSS value is declared once, project-wide, in `app/assets/css/main.css`'s
`--chat-font-sans` and applied to the whole overlay via `body.chat`'s
`--font-family-sans: var(--chat-font-sans)`. `PureChatList.vue` itself sets
neither `font-family` nor `font-size` — both are inherited defaults from that
page-level rule (`fontSize: 1.8rem` here mirrors `body.chat`'s
`--font-size: 1.8rem`). The one property this theme _does_ set locally is
`lineHeight: 2.5rem` — a literal, absolute row height on `.item`, not a
unitless multiplier — chosen to keep stacked chat lines close without
letting outlined glyphs from adjacent lines touch. `fontWeight: 400` is the
plain body weight; nothing in this theme is ever bold, because there is no
nickname left to distinguish from the message by weight.

Every message is rendered through `TextWithShadow` with `shadow-size="0.1"`,
producing the same thin, hard, 8-direction black outline used by `default`
and `simple`. There is no `components.*` property for a text outline in this
schema, so — as in those themes' own files — it is documented here in prose
rather than forced into a fake token.

## Layout

`.chat-container` scopes one custom property that backs a token in this file:
`--dot-size: 1.2rem` is `{spacing.dot-size}`, `identity-dot`'s width and height.
It is declared locally to `.chat-container` rather than promoted to a shared,
project-wide custom property, because it is this theme's own decision, not a
cross-theme invariant — no other theme has an identity dot at all.

Two `0.8rem` values in `PureChatList.vue` happen to coincide but are recorded,
in the component's own comment, as separate decisions that should stay
separate: `.item`'s `margin: 0.4rem 0.8rem` is the outer gutter between
stacked chat items, while `.nickname-icon`'s `margin-right: 0.8rem` is the gap
between the dot and the start of the message text. Neither has a home in the
`components.*` schema (there is no `margin` or `gap` property), so neither is
declared as a front-matter token — and neither should be collapsed into one
shared value just because the numbers currently match; that would fabricate a
shared design decision that was never made. The container itself
(`.chat-container`) is a full-viewport (`100vw`/`100vh`) positioning context,
and `.list` is pinned to its bottom-left corner via
`position: absolute; left: 0; right: 0; bottom: 0` — the same bottom-anchored
stacking behavior every theme in this project shares.

This theme renders **no platform icon and no badges at all** — unlike
`default`, `simple`, `colorful`, and the `cute-*` themes, which all gate a
platform icon behind `v-if="!chatOptions.isHidePlatformIcon"`,
`PureChatList.vue`'s template has no icon element to gate in the first place.
`isHidePlatformIcon` is simply inert here: setting it changes nothing, because
there was never anything for it to hide. That is consistent with this theme's
whole premise — it already strips identity down past the point where a
platform badge would fit.

## Elevation & Depth

There is no elevation cue anywhere in this theme — no plate, no shadow, no
opaque surface of any kind. `identity-dot`'s `{colors.primary}` fill and the
message text both sit directly on raw, uncontrolled video. The only thing
standing in for depth is the hard outline described under Typography, which
guarantees legibility without implying a surface.

## Shapes

`{rounded.dot}` (`0.9rem`) applied to a `{spacing.dot-size}` (`1.2rem`) square
produces a true circle — the same circle-via-matching-radius trick used
elsewhere in this project for round elements. Around that circle,
`.nickname-icon` also carries a `0.2rem solid rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.1)` ring, which
is a `border`, and this schema has no `border`/`borderColor` property to
express it — it is recorded here rather than invented as a fake token. The
ring's job is to keep light-hued dots (high lightness at any hue, since
`hashToColor` always fixes lightness at `70%`) from disappearing into a
bright patch of video; a thin, near-black edge holds the circle's shape
regardless of what hue landed inside it. The message itself sets no
`border-radius` at all — there is no box around it to round.

## Components

- `identity-dot` — the entire identity system of this theme: a
  `{spacing.dot-size}` circle (`{rounded.dot}`) filled with `{colors.primary}`,
  one sample of the per-author hashed-hue family described under Colors; also
  carries the `0.2rem` dark ring noted under Shapes, which this schema cannot
  express as a token.
- `message` — the only other visible element, in `{colors.text}` at
  `{typography.message}`, rendered through `TextWithShadow`'s hard outline;
  deliberately declares no `backgroundColor`, because this theme has no
  background to pair it with.
- `emoji` — mirrors the project-wide `--chat-icon-size: 1.8rem` custom
  property declared once in `app/assets/css/main.css` and consumed by every
  theme. `{spacing.icon}` is a copy of that single source of truth, kept
  here only because token references resolve solely within this file — it
  must track `--chat-icon-size`, never diverge from it locally. This theme has
  no `icon` or `badge` component to go with it, because it renders neither
  (see Layout).
- `sticker` — mirrors the same file's `--chat-sticker-size: 10rem` the same
  way.

## Do's and Don'ts

- Do treat `{colors.primary}` as one sample of a 360-hue generated family, not
  a fixed brand color. Don't replace `hashToColor`'s hue derivation with a
  curated palette — that would be `colorful`'s design, not this one.
- Do accept that two authors can land on the same hue (`hash % 360`). Don't
  "fix" this by widening the dot to carry a second differentiator (initials, a
  pattern, a border color per author) — the smallness of the identity system
  is the design, and it is only sound for a small, mostly-recurring roster.
- Do keep `message` free of any `backgroundColor`. Don't add a plate "to be
  safe" — the hard outline is this theme's actual, and only, legibility
  mechanism, and a plate would contradict the stripped-down premise the same
  way restoring the nickname would.
- Do leave `isHidePlatformIcon` unimplemented here. Don't add a platform icon
  to this theme to make the option "do something" — this theme never had one,
  and adding one now would be restoring identity information the design
  deliberately removed.
- Do keep `--dot-size` scoped to this theme's own `.chat-container`. Don't
  promote it to a shared, project-wide custom property — no other theme has an
  identity dot, so there is nothing to share it with.
